stem: The spouse caring for a client with advanced cancer says, 'I am sleeping only a few hours, missing work, and I am afraid I will make a mistake with the medications because I am exhausted.' Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.A: Assess the caregiver's immediate safety and caregiving capacity, identify tasks that can be shared, and connect the family with available respite, social-work, and practical support resources.
options.B: Encourage the spouse to continue all caregiving duties alone because accepting outside help usually increases caregiver stress.
options.C: Reassure the spouse that severe exhaustion is an expected part of caregiving and does not need intervention unless the client is hospitalized.
options.D: Focus only on the client's needs because caregiver sleep, work strain, and medication-management concerns are outside the nursing plan of care.

rationale: Cancer caregiving can create substantial physical, emotional, practical, and financial strain. NCI advises caregivers to take an honest look at what they can and cannot safely do, share or delegate tasks when possible, and seek help rather than waiting until they are overwhelmed. Respite care, social-work assistance, family/friend support, counseling, and other resources may help preserve caregiver well-being and the safety of care provided to the client. Severe sleep loss combined with concern about medication errors is a concrete safety signal, so the nurse should assess capacity and mobilize support rather than normalize exhaustion or exclude caregiver needs from care planning.
educational_objective: Recognize clinically significant cancer-caregiver burden when exhaustion threatens caregiver health or safe medication management and coordinate practical, respite, and psychosocial support.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Caregivers of Cancer Patients; Taking Care of Yourself — Advanced Cancer and Caregivers
source_locator: Caregivers of Cancer Patients — accepting help and sharing tasks; Taking Care of Yourself — guilt, caregiver overload, getting help, and respite care
source_claim_supported: NCI recognizes the sustained demands and stress of cancer caregiving, advises caregivers to identify what they can and cannot do, share tasks, accept help, and consider respite or professional support when overwhelmed.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — family/caregiver coping, support systems, stress management, therapeutic communication, and referral for psychosocial resources
blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — caregiver burden affecting safety and coping in advanced cancer
correction_summary: Rebuilt the original caregiver-burden definition item into an applied safety and support scenario. Added sleep deprivation, work disruption, and fear of medication error to make burden clinically actionable, and required assessment plus task-sharing, respite, social-work, and support-resource coordination rather than merely recognizing that burden exists.
audit_findings: Original item defined caregiver burden but did not test a nursing decision or distinguish distress from a safety-threatening level of exhaustion.
Fresh NCI review directly supports assessing caregiver limitations, sharing tasks, accepting help, and using respite/support resources.
The final item makes medication-error concern an explicit reason to intervene without claiming that every tired caregiver requires the same service package.
Caregiver needs are included because caregiver capacity can directly affect both family well-being and safe home care.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct action with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, normalization of unsafe exhaustion, or unresolved source conflict.
